nodes.title: Change in Accounting Principle
nodes.heading: C. Change in Accounting Principle
nodes.start_phrase: In the first quarter of 2021, we adopted a change in accoun ting principle to a more preferable policy under U.S. GAAP to immediately recognize actuarial gains and losses arising fromthe remeasurement of our pension and postretirement plans (MTM Accounting).
nodes.summary:
- Basis of presentation under U.S. GAAP: consolidation based on voting interests and effective control; elimination of intercompany transactions; differing year-ends for U.S. (Dec 31) and non-U.S. (Nov 30) subsidiaries; most unremitted foreign earnings not restricted; rounding/reclassification notes.
- Business portfolio changes and discontinued operations: 2021 reorganization into two operating segments (Biopharma and PC1); sale of Meridian (EpiPen) with results presented as discontinued operations; termination of Mylan-Japan collaboration and transfer to Viatris; 2020 spin-off and combination of Upjohn with Mylan to form Viatris with Upjohn results in discontinued operations and related balance sheet derecognition and equity presentation; prior-period reclassifications and impacts from other 2019–2021 acquisitions.
- New 2021 accounting standard adoption (income taxes): removal of certain exceptions for intraperiod tax allocation, interim tax calculations, outside basis differences, franchise taxes, and enacted tax law changes; no material impact.
- Change in accounting principle (Q1 2021): adoption of mark-to-market recognition for pension and postretirement actuarial gains/losses (MTM Accounting), recorded immediately in Other (income)/deductions—net; retrospective application with a $6.0 billion cumulative decrease to Retained earnings and offset to Accumulated other comprehensive loss; rationale includes improved transparency and alignment with fair value principles.
- Quantitative impacts of the accounting change: summarized effects on income statement (other income/deductions, income before taxes, tax provision, EPS), comprehensive income (OCI components and taxes), cash flows (deferred taxes, benefit plan contributions), and balance sheet (deferred tax assets, pension obligations, retained earnings, AOCI).
- Use of estimates and assumptions: pervasive across revenue deductions, inventory costs, depreciation/amortization, restructuring, contingencies, taxes, valuations, impairment reviews, acquisitions, investments, financial instruments, valuation allowances, pensions/postretirement, share-based compensation; subject to uncertainty and updated as needed.
- Acquisitions accounting: acquisition method with assets/liabilities (including IPR&D) at fair value; transaction costs expensed; goodwill recognized for excess consideration; asset acquisitions that are not businesses result in IPR&D expensed in R&D and no goodwill; contingent consideration initially at fair value (probability-weighted DCF) and remeasured through earnings in Other (income)/deductions—net.
- Fair value measurement framework: exit price notion considering market participants, highest and best use, and nonperformance risk; valuation approaches (income, market, cost) and fair value hierarchy (Levels 1–3); instrument-specific methods (AFS debt via matrix pricing and credit-adjusted curves; equity via quoted/NAV prices; derivatives via models using observable inputs like interest rate curves and FX prices; money market funds via NAV); ongoing validation of third-party pricing models and inputs.

nodes.title: Estimates and Assumptions
nodes.heading: D. Estimates and Assumptions
nodes.start_phrase: In preparing these financial statements, we use certain estimates and assumptions that affec t reported amounts and disclosures.
nodes.summary:
The excerpt outlines key accounting policies in Pfizer’s consolidated financial statements. It explains the pervasive use of estimates and assumptions across income statements and balance sheets, including for revenue deductions, inventory costing, depreciation and amortization, restructuring, contingencies, income taxes, asset valuation and recoverability, and liabilities. It highlights judgment-intensive areas—fair value measurements, acquisition accounting, impairment reviews, restructuring charges, investments and financial instruments, valuation allowances, pension and postretirement plans, contingencies, and share-based compensation—emphasizing inherent uncertainty, potential material impacts if estimates differ from outcomes, and ongoing reassessment in light of changing market, legal, and regulatory conditions.

It details acquisition accounting under the acquisition method: recognizing most acquired assets and assumed liabilities at fair value at the acquisition date; recording acquired IPR&D on the balance sheet; expensing transaction costs; recognizing goodwill for consideration in excess of net identifiable assets; and, for asset acquisitions that are not businesses under U.S. GAAP, recognizing no goodwill and expensing IPR&D to R&D. Contingent consideration is initially measured at fair value (often via probability‑weighted discounted cash flows) and remeasured each period through earnings in Other (income)/deductions—net.

It describes fair value measurement principles using an exit price notion from a market participant perspective, including the highest and best use for non‑financial assets and consistent nonperformance risk for liabilities. It outlines valuation techniques (income, market, and cost approaches) and the fair value hierarchy (Levels 1–3). It specifies methodologies for key instruments: available‑for‑sale debt securities (third‑party matrix pricing with observable inputs and credit‑adjusted yield curves), equity securities with readily determinable fair values (quoted prices/observable NAV), derivatives (third‑party models using observable inputs like yield curves and FX forwards/spots; limited credit risk impact), and money market funds (observable NAV). Pfizer also describes controls over third‑party pricing, including model reviews, input monitoring, and test comparisons to actual trades.

nodes.title: Acquisitions
nodes.heading: E. Acquisitions
nodes.start_phrase: Our consolidated financial statements include the operations of acquired businesses after the completion of the acquisitions.
nodes.summary:
- Scope: Notes to Consolidated Financial Statements (Pfizer) covering Estimates and Assumptions (D), Acquisitions (E), and Fair Value (F).
- Estimates and assumptions: Used broadly across income statement and balance sheet items, including revenue deductions, inventory costing, depreciation/amortization, restructuring, contingencies, tax provisions, asset valuation/recoverability, and liabilities. Fair value estimates affect acquisitions, impairment reviews, investments/financial instruments, valuation allowances, pension/postretirement plans, contingencies, and share-based compensation. Estimates involve complex, judgment-based assessments of uncertain future events; results may differ due to risks such as healthcare changes, competition, litigation, and regulation. Estimates are regularly evaluated and adjusted as facts change.
- Acquisitions accounting: Consolidate acquired businesses from the acquisition date using the acquisition method; recognize most assets and liabilities at fair value, record acquired IPR&D on the balance sheet, expense transaction costs, and record goodwill for consideration exceeding identifiable net assets. If acquiring net assets that are not a U.S. GAAP “business,” no goodwill is recorded and acquired IPR&D is expensed to R&D. Contingent consideration is measured at fair value at acquisition (typically via probability-weighted DCF), remeasured each reporting period, with changes recognized in Other (income)/deductions—net.
- Fair value measurement: Apply an exit price notion from a market participant perspective, considering highest and best use for non-financial assets and consistent nonperformance risk for liabilities. Use income, market, and cost approaches, with a three-level input hierarchy (Level 1: quoted prices; Level 2: observable inputs; Level 3: unobservable inputs). Specific methods: AFS debt securities via third-party matrix pricing with observable data and credit-adjusted curves; equity securities via quoted prices/NAV; derivatives via third-party matrix models using observable yield curves and currency prices (credit risk impact not significant); money market funds via observable NAV. The company reviews third-party pricing methodologies and inputs for reasonableness through cross-checks, monitoring key inputs, and test comparisons to actual trades.

nodes.title: Fair Value
nodes.heading: F. Fair Value
nodes.start_phrase: We measure certain assets and liabilities at fair value, either upon initial recognition or for subsequent accounting or reporting.
nodes.summary:
- Estimates and assumptions: Financial statements rely on significant judgments affecting revenue deductions, inventory costs, depreciation/amortization, restructuring, contingencies, taxes, asset valuation/recoverability, impairments, investments, financial instruments, valuation allowances, pensions/postretirement, and share-based compensation. Estimates are updated regularly; outcomes may differ due to industry, legal, competitive, and regulatory changes.

- Acquisitions: Accounted for using the acquisition method, recognizing most acquired assets and assumed liabilities at fair value on the acquisition date; acquired IPR&D recorded on the balance sheet. Transaction costs are expensed. Goodwill is the excess purchase price over net identifiable assets. Asset acquisitions that are not a business recognize no goodwill and expense IPR&D to R&D. Contingent consideration is measured at fair value at acquisition and remeasured through earnings (Other (income)/deductions—net).

- Fair value: Measured using an exit price from a market participant perspective; techniques include income, market, and cost approaches. Uses a three-level input hierarchy (Levels 1–3). Methods include matrix pricing for AFS debt securities and derivatives, quoted/observable NAV prices for equity and money market funds; credit risk on derivatives not significant. Third-party pricing is periodically validated.

- Foreign currency: Functional currency financials translated to USD at period-end (balance sheet) and average (income statement) rates; translation effects in OCI. Remeasurement of non-functional currency monetary items in Other (income)/deductions—net. Highly inflationary economies: monetary items at current rates; non-monetary at historical rates.

- Revenues and receivables: Recognize product revenue upon transfer of control (typically shipment/delivery and title transfer). Sales are subject to variable consideration (chargebacks, rebates, sales allowances/returns, cash discounts) estimated in-period. Sales return provisions consider policies, history, shelf life, lag time, LOE, recalls, competition. Sales incentives reduce revenue when recognized/offered, estimated from historical experience.

- Sales arrangements/customers: Products sold to wholesalers, retailers, hospitals, clinics, government agencies, pharmacies; vaccines largely to governments/ institutions. U.S.: contracts with distributors/hospitals, managed care/PBMs, and mandated government rebates; rebates/coverage gap discounts estimated using experience ratios and current terms. Outside U.S.: allowances primarily contractual/legislated, estimated from invoiced sales; some EU rebates tied to budget overages or thresholds, supported by third-party data. Chargebacks settle within 2–5 weeks and closely match actuals.

- Concentration and IP: A significant share of revenue comes from a limited number of high-selling products; revenue concentration increased from 2019 to 2021. Loss/expiration of IP can materially reduce prices/volumes and increase sales returns around LOE.

nodes.title: Foreign Currency Translation
nodes.heading: G. Foreign Currency Translation
nodes.start_phrase: For most of our international operations, local currencies have been determined to be the functional currencies.
nodes.summary:
- Foreign currency translation policy: use local functional currencies; translate assets/liabilities at period-end rates and income/expense at average rates; translation effects to Other comprehensive income/(loss); remeasurement of non-functional currency monetary items and all monetary items in highly inflationary economies to Other (income)/deductions—net; non-monetary items in highly inflationary economies kept at historical rates.
- Revenue recognition and trade receivables: recognize product sales upon transfer of control (generally at shipment/delivery and title passage); credit sales under short-term terms; revenues reduced for allowances, chargebacks, rebates, returns, and cash discounts; estimate variable consideration in the period of sale.
- Provisions and estimates: detailed methodology for sales returns (local policies, historical returns, reasons, shelf life, lag time, LOE, recalls, competitive changes); sales incentives recorded as revenue reductions and estimated from historical program experience.
- Sales channels and customers: Rx products primarily to wholesalers and also to retailers, hospitals, clinics, government agencies, pharmacies; U.S. vaccines sold to federal government/CDC, wholesalers, providers, pharmacies, IDNs; ex-U.S. vaccines sold mainly to governmental and non-governmental institutions; products used by patients often subject to government/managed care/PBM programs with negotiated or legislated rebates/allowances.
- U.S.-specific deductions: contracts with distributors/hospitals, managed care/PBMs, and mandated government rebates (Medicare, Medicaid); rebate accruals based on experience ratios tied to actual prescriptions; Medicare Part D coverage gap discounts estimated from historical utilization; performance-based rebates consider formulary status and rebate rates.
- Outside U.S.: allowances largely contractual/legislated; estimates based on actual invoiced sales; in parts of Europe, rebates tied to unbudgeted spend or sales thresholds using allocation factors; third-party data used to monitor accrual adequacy.
- Chargebacks: primarily U.S. wholesaler reimbursements for contracted/legislated prices; settled within 2–5 weeks; accruals closely match actuals.
- Product concentration: count of products exceeding $1B in direct sales/alliance revenues for 2019–2021 and their share of total revenues, with cross-reference to Note 17B.
- Impact of loss/expiration of intellectual property: expected revenue declines from lower prices/volumes due to generic competition; higher sales return provisions as LOE approaches.

nodes.title: Revenues and Trade Accounts Receivable
nodes.heading: H. Revenues and Trade Accounts Receivable
nodes.start_phrase: We record revenues from product sales when there is a transfer of control of the product from us to the customer.
nodes.summary:
- Foreign currency translation: Most international subsidiaries use local functional currencies. Assets/liabilities translated at period-end rates; income/expenses at average rates; translation differences to Other comprehensive income/(loss). Remeasurement of non-functional currency monetary items goes to Other (income)/deductions—net. In highly inflationary economies, monetary items are translated at current rates with adjustments to Other (income)/deductions—net; non-monetary items at historical rates.
- Revenue recognition and contracts: Product revenue recognized upon transfer of control (typically shipment or delivery when title passes). Sales on credit are short term; collections follow market norms. Revenues are reduced for variable consideration (chargebacks, rebates, sales allowances/returns, cash discounts), estimated in the period of sale using judgment and historical/current factors.
- Sales returns and incentives: Return provisions are market- and product-specific, considering policies, historical return rates, causes of returns, shelf life, lag times, LOE, recalls, and competition. Returned products are generally destroyed with credits issued. Sales incentives reduce revenue when the related revenue is recognized or when offered, estimated using historical behavior.
- Customers and payer arrangements: Products are sold to wholesalers, retailers, hospitals, clinics, government agencies, and pharmacies. U.S. vaccines are sold to federal government/CDC, wholesalers, providers, pharmacies, and IDNs; outside the U.S., primarily to government/non-government institutions. U.S. rebates include managed care/PBM contracts and mandated federal/state programs (Medicare, Medicaid), estimated using experience ratios updated regularly; Medicare Part D coverage gap discounts estimated based on historical and expected utilization. Outside the U.S., many allowances are contractual/mandated and based on invoiced sales; some European rebates tied to budget overruns or thresholds using allocation factors and third-party data. Chargebacks (mainly U.S.) closely approximate actuals and are settled within two to five weeks.
- Revenue concentration and LOE: Direct product sales and/or alliance revenues exceeded $1B for 9 products in 2021 (7 in 2020; 6 in 2019), totaling 75% of 2021 revenue (54% in 2020; 49% in 2019). Loss or expiration of IP can significantly reduce prices/volumes; higher sales return provisions are recorded as LOE approaches in markets.
- Sales-related accruals: As of Dec 31 (millions) — 2021 vs. 2020: Reserve against trade A/R, net of allowance: $1,077 vs. $861; Other current liabilities—Accrued rebates: $3,811 vs. $3,017; Other accruals: $528 vs. $432; Other noncurrent liabilities: $433 vs. $399; Total accrued rebates and other sales-related accruals: $5,850 vs. $4,708. Taxes collected from customers and remitted to authorities are excluded from Revenues.
- Trade accounts receivable and credit losses: A/R are at net realizable value. Allowance for credit losses is based on historical experience, current information, and macroeconomic forecasts. Receivables are pooled by market (U.S./international), delinquency, and customer type (risk level; government/non-government) with fixed reserve percentages. Credit risk indicators and reserves are reviewed quarterly by region; write-offs occur after all collection efforts (including litigation) are exhausted. Additions, write-offs, and recoveries in 2021/2020 were not material.
- Collaborative arrangements accounting: Presentation depends on contract terms, payment nature, and guidance. Co-promotion: share of partners’ gross profits recorded as alliance revenues as services are performed; related selling/marketing reimbursements in Selling, informational and administrative (SI&A) expenses. If Pfizer manufactures, revenue recognized upon transfer of control to partner. If Pfizer is principal, partner profit shares and royalties paid are in Cost of sales; royalties received are in Other (income)/deductions—net. Development cost reimbursements flow through R&D expenses. Upfront and pre-approval milestones paid by Pfizer are expensed to R&D; post-approval milestones paid are capitalized to Identifiable intangible assets—Developed technology rights. Upfront/pre-approval milestones earned by Pfizer are recognized in Other (income)/deductions—net over the development period when R&D services are performance obligations; other milestones may be recognized immediately or over time depending on obligations. Regulatory approval milestones are generally included in the transaction price when approval is attained, or earlier if reversal is not probable.
- Cost of sales and inventories: Inventories carried at lower of cost or net realizable value; cost determined using average actual cost for finished goods, WIP, and raw materials. Inventories are reviewed regularly and reserved for impairment when necessary.
- Selling, informational and administrative expenses: Expensed as incurred, including marketing, advertising, shipping/handling, IT, and legal defense. Advertising expense: approximately $2.0B (2021), $1.8B (2020), $2.3B (2019). Production costs expensed as incurred; media spend expensed when aired/published.

nodes.title: Collaborative Arrangements
nodes.heading: I. Collaborative Arrangements
nodes.start_phrase: Payments to and from our collaboration partners are presented in our consolidated statements of income based on the nature o f the arrangement (including its contractual terms), thenature of the payments and applicable accounting guidance.
nodes.summary:
- Sales-related accruals: As of December 31, 2021 (vs. 2020), reserves included $1,077M ($861M) against trade accounts receivable, accrued rebates of $3,811M ($3,017M), other accruals of $528M ($432M), and other noncurrent liabilities of $433M ($399M), totaling $5,850M ($4,708M). Taxes collected from customers and remitted to governments are excluded from Revenues.

- Trade accounts receivable and credit losses: Receivables are recorded at net realizable value. Allowances for expected credit losses are estimated using historical data, current conditions, and forward-looking factors. Receivables are pooled by market (U.S./international), delinquency, and customer type (risk level; government/non-government) with fixed reserve percentages informed by regulatory/legal environments, country/political risk, and macroeconomic indicators. Reserves are reviewed quarterly; specific troubled accounts receive additional allowances; write-offs occur after collection efforts are exhausted. Additions/write-offs/recoveries in 2021 and 2020 were not material.

- Collaborative arrangements accounting:
  - Co-promotion where partner is principal: Pfizer records alliance revenues (within Revenues) for its share of partner net sales/profits as co-promotion services are performed; related selling costs and reimbursements are in Selling, informational and administrative expenses.
  - Manufacturing for partners: Revenue recognized upon transfer of control of product to partner.
  - When Pfizer is principal: Payments to partners for their share of net sales/profits and all royalties to partners are in Cost of sales; royalties received from partners are in Other (income)/deductions—net.
  - R&D cost reimbursements are recorded in Research and development expenses.
  - Upfront and pre-approval milestone payments Pfizer owes in development stage are expensed to R&D; post-approval milestones Pfizer owes are capitalized to Identifiable intangible assets—Developed technology rights.
  - Upfront/pre-approval milestone payments earned by Pfizer are recognized in Other (income)/deductions—net over the development period when performance obligations include R&D services, or immediately/over other periods depending on obligations. Milestones tied to regulatory approval are generally recognized when approval is attained; earlier recognition is possible if a significant reversal is not probable.

- Cost of sales and inventories: Inventories are carried at the lower of cost or net realizable value; costs (finished goods, WIP, raw materials) use average actual cost. Inventories are reviewed regularly for impairment and reserves recorded as needed.

- Selling, informational and administrative expenses: Expensed as incurred, covering marketing, advertising, shipping/handling, IT, and legal defense. Advertising expense was ~$2.0B (2021), $1.8B (2020), $2.3B (2019). Production costs are expensed as incurred; media placement costs are expensed when the advertising occurs.

nodes.title: Cost of Sales and Inventories
nodes.heading: J. Cost of Sales and Inventories
nodes.start_phrase: Inventories are recorded at the lower of cost or net realizable value.
nodes.summary:
- Summarizes Pfizer’s sales-related accruals as of December 31, 2021 and 2020, including reserves against trade accounts receivable and liabilities for rebates, other accruals, and noncurrent items, totaling $5,850 million in 2021 vs. $4,708 million in 2020 (key components: reserve against trade AR $1,077m vs. $861m; accrued rebates $3,811m vs. $3,017m; other accruals $528m vs. $432m; other noncurrent liabilities $433m vs. $399m).
- Notes that taxes collected from customers on product sales are excluded from Revenues.
- Describes trade accounts receivable and credit loss accounting: receivables at net realizable value; expected credit loss allowances based on historical experience, current conditions, and forecasts; segmentation by market (U.S./international), delinquency, and customer type (risk level, government/non-government) with fixed reserve percentages; quarterly monitoring and adjustments; specific allowances for known troubled accounts; write-offs after collection efforts are exhausted; 2021 and 2020 credit loss activity not material.
- Details accounting for collaborative arrangements:
  - Co-promotion: Pfizer records its share of partner gross profits as alliance revenues when the partner is principal; related selling/marketing costs and reimbursements in SG&A.
  - Manufacturing for partners: revenue recognized upon transfer of control.
  - When Pfizer is principal: partner profit shares and royalties paid recorded in Cost of sales; royalties received recorded in Other (income)/deductions—net.
  - Development cost reimbursements recorded in R&D expenses.
  - Upfront and pre-approval milestones paid by Pfizer expensed to R&D; post-approval milestones paid capitalized to Identifiable intangible assets—Developed technology rights.
  - Upfront/pre-approval milestones earned by Pfizer recognized in Other (income)/deductions—net over the development period when R&D services are performance obligations; other milestones may be recognized immediately or over time depending on obligations; regulatory approval milestones generally recognized when approval is attained, with earlier recognition possible if reversal is not probable.
- Outlines inventory accounting: lower of cost or net realizable value; average actual cost; regular impairment reviews and reserves as needed.
- Explains selling, informational and administrative expenses: expensed as incurred; include marketing, advertising, shipping/handling, IT, and legal defense; advertising expenses were about $2.0B (2021), $1.8B (2020), and $2.3B (2019); production costs expensed as incurred; media placement costs expensed when ads run.

nodes.title: Selling, Informational and Administrative Expenses
nodes.heading: K. Selling, Informational and Administrative Expenses
nodes.start_phrase: Selling, informational and administrative costs are expensed as incurred.
nodes.summary:
- Accruals for sales-related deductions: Details the reserve balances and classifications for Medicare/Medicaid and other rebates, chargebacks, sales allowances/returns, and cash discounts as of December 31, 2021 and 2020 (total $5,850 million vs. $4,708 million), including amounts against trade receivables and in current/noncurrent liabilities; notes that taxes collected from customers are excluded from Revenues.
- Trade accounts receivable and credit losses: Receivables stated at net realizable value; allowance for expected credit losses based on pooled segmentation (market, delinquency, customer type), fixed reserve percentages informed by history, regulatory/legal and country risk, and macroeconomic forecasts; quarterly monitoring and adjustments; specific allowances for known troubled accounts; write-offs after exhaustive collection efforts; 2021 and 2020 movements immaterial.
- Collaborative arrangements accounting: Revenue and cost presentation based on contract terms and principal/agent assessment. Co-promotion gross profit shares recorded as alliance revenues; related selling/marketing costs in SG&A. Manufacturing for partners recognized on transfer of control. When Pfizer is principal, partner profit shares and royalties paid recorded in Cost of sales; royalties received recorded in Other (income)/deductions—net. R&D cost reimbursements in R&D. Upfront and pre-approval milestones paid by Pfizer expensed to R&D; post-approval milestones capitalized as developed technology rights. Upfront/milestone payments earned by Pfizer recognized in Other (income)/deductions—net immediately or over time depending on performance obligations; regulatory milestones generally recognized upon approval (or earlier if reversal not probable).
- Cost of sales and inventories: Inventories at lower of cost or net realizable value using average actual cost; regular impairment review.
- Selling, informational and administrative expenses: Expensed as incurred; include marketing, advertising, shipping/handling, IT, legal defense. Advertising expense was ~$2.0B (2021), $1.8B (2020), $2.3B (2019); production costs expensed as incurred; media costs expensed when ads run.
- Research and development expenses: Expensed as incurred, including licensing. Pre-approval upfront/milestone payments expensed; post-approval milestones capitalized to identifiable intangible assets and typically amortized straight-line over the remaining term or expected product life.
- Amortization, depreciation, and long-lived assets: PP&E at cost, depreciated straight-line; identifiable intangibles at acquisition-date fair value—finite-lived amortized, indefinite-lived not amortized; goodwill not amortized. Amortization and depreciation presented in Cost of sales, SG&A, R&D, or Amortization of intangible assets depending on function. Impairment testing: finite-lived and other long-lived assets tested upon indicators (undiscounted cash flows; write down to fair value if needed); indefinite-lived intangibles and goodwill tested at least annually (write down if fair value below carrying); reassess useful lives and indefinite-life classification as appropriate.
- Restructuring, acquisition-related, and productivity initiative costs: Recognizes charges for integration, restructuring, site rationalization, workforce reductions, shared services/global systems; included in Restructuring charges and certain acquisition-related costs. Changes to useful lives flow through functional expense lines. Employee termination costs accrued when probable/estimable; transaction costs expensed as incurred. Notes potential impact across commercial, manufacturing, R&D, and corporate enabling functions.
- Cash equivalents and cash flows: Cash equivalents are highly liquid investments with original maturities of three months or less; if part of a larger pool, presented as short-term investments.

nodes.title: Research and Development Expenses
nodes.heading: L. Research and Development Expenses
nodes.start_phrase: R&D costs are expensed as incurred.
nodes.summary:
- Research and Development Expenses: R&D costs are expensed as incurred, including proprietary efforts and certain licensing costs. Before regulatory approval, upfront and milestone payments under licenses are expensed (upfront when incurred; milestones when achieved). After approval, milestone payments are capitalized as identifiable intangible assets and typically amortized straight-line over the shorter of remaining agreement term or expected product life, unless deemed indefinite-lived.

- Amortization, Depreciation, and Long-Lived Assets: 
  - Property, plant and equipment recorded at cost (including significant improvements) and depreciated straight-line over estimated useful lives; tax depreciation may be accelerated.
  - Identifiable intangible assets recorded at fair value at acquisition; finite-lived intangibles amortized straight-line; indefinite-lived intangibles not amortized until life determinable.
  - Goodwill not amortized.
  - Income statement classification: multi-function finite-lived intangible amortization in “Amortization of intangible assets”; single-function intangible amortization and PP&E depreciation in Cost of sales, SG&A, and/or R&D, as appropriate.
  - Impairment: ongoing monitoring; annual testing for goodwill and indefinite-lived intangibles. For finite-lived assets/PP&E, test upon indicators using undiscounted cash flows; impair to fair value if needed and reassess useful lives. For indefinite-lived intangibles (brands, IPR&D), impair excess of book over fair value and reassess indefinite-life status (except IPR&D). For goodwill, compare reporting unit book value to implied fair value.

- Restructuring and Acquisition-Related Costs: 
  - Costs arise from acquisitions (transaction execution, integration, restructuring) and productivity initiatives (site/facility rationalizations, workforce reductions, shared services/global systems).
  - Recognized in “Restructuring charges and certain acquisition-related costs.” Changes to asset useful lives from actions flow to Cost of sales, SG&A, and/or R&D.
  - Employee termination costs recorded when probable and estimable; may be paid over time. Transaction costs (banking, legal, accounting) expensed as incurred.
  - Potential impacts across commercial, manufacturing, R&D, and corporate enabling functions.

- Cash Equivalents and Cash Flows: Cash equivalents include highly liquid instruments (e.g., CDs, time deposits) with original maturities of three months or less; if part of a larger investment pool, classified as short-term investments.

nodes.title: Amortization of Intangible Assets, Depreciation and Certain Long-Lived Assets
nodes.heading: M. Amortization of Intangible Assets, Depreciation and Certain Long-Lived Assets
nodes.start_phrase: These assets are recorded at cost, including any significant improvements after purchase, less accumulated depreciation.
nodes.summary:
- Research and development (R&D) costs are expensed as incurred, including proprietary R&D and certain licensing costs. Upfront and milestone payments before regulatory approval are expensed; after approval, milestone payments are capitalized as identifiable intangible assets and amortized straight-line over the shorter of the remaining agreement term or expected product life, unless the asset is indefinite-lived.
- Property, plant and equipment (PP&E) are recorded at cost and depreciated straight-line over estimated useful lives (tax depreciation may be accelerated). Depreciation starts when assets are ready for intended use.
- Identifiable intangible assets acquired are recorded at fair value. Finite-lived intangibles are amortized straight-line; indefinite-lived intangibles are not amortized until a life can be determined.
- Goodwill represents purchase consideration in excess of net assets acquired and is not amortized.
- Expense classification: amortization of finite-lived acquired intangibles benefiting multiple functions is presented in Amortization of intangible assets; single-function intangibles’ amortization and PP&E depreciation are included in Cost of sales, Selling, informational and administrative expenses, and/or Research and development expenses, as appropriate.
- Impairment reviews: long-lived assets are monitored for indicators; indefinite-lived intangibles and goodwill are tested at least annually.
  - Finite-lived intangibles and other long-lived assets: if indicators exist, compare undiscounted cash flows to carrying amount; if not recoverable, write down to fair value and reassess useful lives.
  - Indefinite-lived intangibles (brands, IPR&D): measure fair value; record impairment if carrying value exceeds fair value, and reassess indefinite-life classification (except IPR&D).
  - Goodwill: compare reporting unit’s carrying value to its implied fair value; record impairment if carrying exceeds fair value.
- Restructuring and acquisition-related costs: may arise from acquisitions and cost-reduction/productivity programs (e.g., site closures, workforce reductions, facility rationalization, shared services, systems integration).
  - Included in Restructuring charges and certain acquisition-related costs are all restructuring charges and certain acquisition integration costs; changes to asset useful lives from restructuring are recorded in relevant operating expense lines.
  - Employee termination costs are recognized when probable and estimable; transaction costs (banking, legal, accounting) for acquisitions are expensed as incurred.
  - Actions can affect commercial, manufacturing, R&D, and corporate enabling functions.
- Cash equivalents are highly liquid investments with original maturities of three months or less; if part of a larger investment pool, they are classified as Short-term investments.

nodes.title: Restructuring Charges and Other Costs Associated with Acquisitions and Cost-Reduction/Productivity Initiatives
nodes.heading: N. Restructuring Charges and Other Costs Associated with Acquisitions and Cost-Reduction/Productivity Initiatives
nodes.start_phrase: We may incur restructuring charges in connection with acquisitions when we implement plans to restructure and integrate the acquired operations or in connection with our cost- reduction and productivity initiatives.
nodes.summary:
- R&D expenses: Expensed as incurred, including proprietary efforts and certain licensing costs. Before regulatory approval, upfront and milestone payments under licensing deals are expensed (upfront when incurred; milestones when achieved). After approval, milestone payments are capitalized to identifiable intangible assets (unless indefinite-lived) and typically amortized straight-line over the shorter of the remaining agreement term or expected product life.

- Long-lived assets accounting:
  - Property, plant and equipment: Recorded at cost (including significant improvements), depreciated straight-line over estimated useful lives starting when ready for use; accelerated methods used for tax.
  - Identifiable intangible assets: Recorded at fair value at acquisition; finite-lived intangibles amortized straight-line; indefinite-lived intangibles not amortized until a useful life is determinable.
  - Goodwill: Excess purchase price over net assets; not amortized.

- Expense classification: Amortization of finite-lived acquired intangibles benefiting multiple functions is recorded in “Amortization of intangible assets.” Amortization of single-function intangibles and PPE depreciation are included in Cost of sales, Selling, informational and administrative expenses, and/or Research and development expenses, as appropriate.

- Impairment testing:
  - Finite-lived intangibles and other long-lived assets: Test upon impairment indicators; compare undiscounted cash flows to carrying amount; if impaired, write down to fair value and reassess useful lives.
  - Indefinite-lived intangibles (e.g., brands, IPR&D): Determine fair value and record impairment for excess carrying value; reassess indefinite-life classification (except for IPR&D).
  - Goodwill: Test at least annually; impair if a reporting unit’s carrying value exceeds its implied fair value.

- Restructuring and acquisition-related costs: Arise from acquisitions and cost-reduction/productivity initiatives. Include transaction execution costs, integration activities, restructuring of combined operations, site/facility rationalizations, workforce reductions, shared services expansion, and global systems development. Recognized in “Restructuring charges and certain acquisition-related costs.” Changes to asset useful lives flow to Cost of sales, SG&A, and/or R&D. Employee termination costs recorded when probable and estimable. Transaction costs (banking, legal, accounting) expensed as incurred. Actions can affect commercial, manufacturing, R&D, and corporate enabling functions.

- Cash equivalents and cash flows: Cash equivalents are highly liquid investments (e.g., CDs, time deposits) with original maturities of three months or less. If such items are part of a larger investment pool, they are classified as Short-term investments.

nodes.title: Cash Equivalents and Statement of Cash Flows
nodes.heading: O. Cash Equivalents and Statement of Cash Flows
nodes.start_phrase: Cash equivalents include items almost as liquid as cash, such as certificates of deposit and time deposits with maturity periods of three months or less when purchased.
nodes.summary:
- Research and development expenses: R&D costs are expensed as incurred, including licensing costs. Before regulatory approval, upfront payments are expensed when incurred and milestones when achieved. After approval, milestone payments are capitalized as identifiable intangible assets (amortized straight-line over the shorter of agreement term or expected product life unless indefinite-lived).

- Amortization, depreciation, and long-lived assets: 
  - Property, plant and equipment recorded at cost and depreciated straight-line over useful lives (accelerated methods for tax); depreciation begins when ready for intended use.
  - Identifiable intangibles recorded at fair value at acquisition; finite-lived intangibles amortized straight-line; indefinite-lived intangibles not amortized until a life is determinable.
  - Goodwill is excess purchase consideration over assigned net assets and is not amortized.
  - Classification: amortization of multi-function finite-lived acquired intangibles in “Amortization of intangible assets”; single-function intangibles’ amortization and PPE depreciation in Cost of sales, Selling, informational and administrative, and/or R&D, as appropriate.
  - Impairment: ongoing monitoring; annual tests for indefinite-lived intangibles and goodwill; other assets when indicators arise. Finite-lived and other long-lived assets use undiscounted cash flow recoverability test, then write down to fair value if impaired and reassess useful lives. Indefinite-lived intangibles measured at fair value with impairment for excess book over fair value and reassessment of indefinite life (except IPR&D). Goodwill tested at the reporting unit level; impair if carrying value exceeds implied fair value.

- Restructuring and acquisition-related costs: Charges may arise from acquisitions (transaction, integration, restructuring) and cost-reduction/productivity programs (site closures, facility rationalization, workforce reductions, shared services/global systems). These are included in “Restructuring charges and certain acquisition-related costs.” Changes to asset useful lives from these actions flow to Cost of sales, SG&A, and/or R&D. Employee termination costs are recognized when probable and estimable. Acquisition transaction costs (banking, legal, accounting) are expensed as incurred. Actions can affect commercial, manufacturing, R&D, and corporate enabling functions.

- Cash equivalents and cash flows: Cash equivalents are highly liquid investments with original maturities of three months or less; if part of a larger pool, classified as short-term investments. Cash flow classification for hedges depends on the hedged item (fair value/cash flow hedges) or the hedging instrument (net investment hedges); non-qualifying derivatives are classified by their purpose and accounting nature.

- Investments and derivatives: Investment classification depends on nature, intent/ability, and influence.
  - Public equities at fair value with changes in Other (income)/deductions—net.
  - Available-for-sale debt at fair value with changes in OCI until realized.
  - Held-to-maturity debt at amortized cost.
  - Private equity without readily determinable fair values and no significant influence measured at cost adjusted for impairment and observable price changes.
  - Equity-method for investments with significant influence; share of results in Other (income)/deductions—net; basis differences allocated to identifiable assets/liabilities and goodwill; initial measurement at fair value of consideration (typically excluding contingent consideration).
  - Realized gains/losses use specific identification.
  - All financial assets evaluated for impairment; record impairment and reset cost basis when declines are identified.
  - Derivatives carried at fair value; changes recognized in Net income or OCI for qualifying hedges.

- Tax assets, liabilities, and contingencies:
  - Current tax assets include tax effects of intercompany inventory transfers (recognized upon third-party sale) and income tax receivables.
  - Deferred taxes recognized on book–tax differences using enacted rates; valuation allowances recorded if recovery is not more likely than not, considering prudent, feasible tax-planning strategies; deferred taxes presented net by jurisdiction in noncurrent assets/liabilities.
  - GILTI policy election to recognize deferred taxes for temporary differences expected to reverse as GILTI.
  - Other noncurrent tax assets relate to potential cross-border relief via competent authority processes; recoverability depends on payments and, in some cases, successful petitions.
  - Other taxes payable include uncertain tax position liabilities and the noncurrent portion of the TCJA repatriation tax payable (election to pay over eight years through 2026).
  - Income tax contingencies use a benefit recognition model: recognize amounts more likely than not to be sustained on technical merits; measure at the largest amount with a >50% likelihood of realization assuming full examination.

nodes.title: Investments and Derivative Financial Instruments
nodes.heading: P. Investments and Derivative Financial Instruments
nodes.start_phrase: The classification of an investment depends on the nature of the investment , our intent and ability to hold the investment, and the degree to which we may exercise influence.
nodes.summary:
- Cash flows for derivative instruments:
  - Hedge-designated derivatives: classified within operating, investing, or financing consistent with the hedged item; net investment hedge cash flows follow the nature of the hedging instrument.
  - Non-hedge-designated derivatives: classified based on purpose and accounting nature.
- Investments accounting policies:
  - Public equity securities: carried at fair value with changes in Other (income)/deductions—net.
  - Available-for-sale debt securities: fair value with unrealized gains/losses in Other comprehensive income until realized.
  - Held-to-maturity debt securities: amortized cost.
  - Private equity without readily determinable fair values and no significant influence: measured at cost, adjusted for impairment and observable price changes in orderly transactions for identical/similar investments.
  - Equity-method investments (significant influence): recognize share of investee results in Other (income)/deductions—net; acquisition cost allocated to identifiable net assets with any excess to goodwill; initial cost typically excludes contingent consideration.
  - Realized gains/losses on sales use specific identification.
  - Regular impairment evaluations for all financial assets; record impairment and reset cost basis when declines are identified.
- Derivative instruments:
  - Carried at fair value across various balance sheet categories; changes recognized in Net income or, for qualifying hedges, in Other comprehensive income (see Note 7A and Note 7E).
- Tax assets and liabilities:
  - Current tax assets: include tax effects from intercompany inventory transfers recognized upon third-party sale and expected income tax receivables (refunds or reductions of future obligations).
  - Deferred taxes: recognized for temporary differences using enacted rates; valuation allowances recorded when deferred tax assets are not considered recoverable, based on estimates of future taxable income and feasible tax-planning strategies; net presentation by jurisdiction in noncurrent balance sheet.
  - GILTI (TCJA): policy election to recognize deferred taxes for temporary differences expected to reverse as GILTI in future years.
  - Other noncurrent tax assets: potential cross-border double-tax relief from competent authority processes; recoverability depends on payments in one jurisdiction and, where applicable, successful claims in another.
  - Other taxes payable (as of Dec 31, 2021 and 2020): include liabilities for uncertain tax positions and the noncurrent portion of the repatriation tax liability payable through 2026 (see Note 5D and Note 5A).
- Income tax contingencies:
  - Apply a benefit recognition model: recognize tax benefits only if a position is more likely than not to be sustained on technical merits; measure recognized benefit as the largest amount with greater than 50% likelihood of being realized upon settlement.

nodes.title: Tax Assets and Liabilities and Income Tax Contingencies
nodes.heading: Q. Tax Assets and Liabilities and Income Tax Contingencies
nodes.start_phrase:
Current tax assets primarily include (i) tax effects for intercompany transfers of inventory within our combined group, which are recognized in the consolidated statements of income when the inventory is sold to a third party and (ii) income tax receivables that are expected to be recovered either via refunds from taxing authorities or reductions to
 future taxobligations.
nodes.summary:
- Cash flow classification for hedging: hedge-related cash flows are presented in operating, investing, or financing based on the hedged item; net investment hedge cash flows follow the nature of the hedging instrument; non-qualifying derivatives are classified by purpose and accounting nature.
- Investments and derivatives:
  - Public equity securities at fair value with changes in Other (income)/deductions—net.
  - Available-for-sale debt at fair value with unrealized changes in OCI until realized.
  - Held-to-maturity debt at amortized cost.
  - Private equity without readily determinable fair values (no significant influence) at cost adjusted for impairment and observable price changes.
  - Equity-method for investments with significant influence; share of earnings in Other (income)/deductions—net; basis differences allocated to identifiable assets/liabilities with residual to goodwill.
  - Realized gains/losses use specific identification; regular impairment evaluations establish new cost bases when impaired.
  - Derivatives at fair value; changes recognized in Net income or, for qualifying hedges, in OCI (see Note 7A/7E).
- Taxes:
  - Current tax assets include intercompany inventory transfer tax effects recognized upon third-party sale and income tax receivables.
  - Deferred taxes recognized on temporary differences using enacted rates; valuation allowances recorded when recovery is not likely, with net noncurrent presentation by jurisdiction.
  - GILTI policy election to recognize deferred taxes for temporary differences expected to reverse as GILTI.
  - Other noncurrent tax assets relate to competent authority (treaty) double-tax relief; recoverability depends on actual payments and successful claims.
  - Other taxes payable include uncertain tax positions and the noncurrent portion of TCJA repatriation tax payable through 2026 (see Notes 5D, 5A).
  - Income tax contingencies follow a benefit recognition model: recognize if more likely than not, measure at the amount >50% likely upon settlement; update for law changes, statute expirations, or audit resolutions; classify as current only if payable within 12 months; interest/penalties in tax provision.
- Pension and postretirement benefits:
  - Global defined benefit and defined contribution plans; U.S. qualified and nonqualified plans plus retiree medical.
  - Recognize over/underfunded status; obligations measured at actuarial present value using assumptions (discount rate, expected asset return, turnover, mortality; plus compensation growth and medical trend/cost sharing as applicable).
  - Plan assets at fair value; components other than service cost recognized in Other (income)/deductions—net.
- Legal and environmental contingencies:
  - Cover patent, product liability, commercial, environmental, government investigations, guarantees/indemnifications.
  - Accrue losses when probable and reasonably estimable; record best estimate or, if none, the low end of the range; recognize insured recoveries when assured.
- Share-based payments:
  - Measured at grant-date fair value; expense amortized straight-line over vesting; costs recorded in Cost of sales, SG&A, and/or R&D.
- Acquisitions:
  - Trillium (Nov 17, 2021): acquired remaining shares for $2.0B net of cash; prior 2% stake; accounted for as an asset acquisition (lead asset TTI-622); recorded $2.1B acquired IPR&D expense in R&D; $2.0B operating cash outflow; acquired ~$256M of assets (mainly cash/investments) and ~$81M liabilities.
  - Array (July 30, 2019): acquired for $11.2B total ($10.9B net of cash); $157M for unvested options expensed as post-closing compensation in restructuring/acquisition-related costs (see Note 3); financed mainly with debt and cash.

- Accounting policies covered:
  - Unrecognized tax benefits: criteria for recognition, classification as current if payable within 12 months, interest/penalties recorded in tax provision, and treatment of settlements/expiring statutes as discrete items; estimates may materially affect results.
  - Pension and postretirement benefits: scope of defined benefit/defined contribution plans, measurement of obligations and plan assets at fair value, key assumptions (discount rate, returns, turnover, mortality, compensation growth, healthcare costs), and presentation of non-service costs in Other (income)/deductions—net.
  - Legal and environmental contingencies: types of exposures (patent, product liability, commercial, environmental, government investigations, guarantees), accrual policy when losses are probable and reasonably estimable, range-of-loss methodology, and insurance recoveries when assured.
  - Share-based payments: fair value accounting, straight-line amortization over vesting, and expense classification (Cost of sales, SG&A, R&D).

- Acquisitions:
  - Trillium (2021): $2.0B cash (net), accounted for as an asset acquisition; $2.1B IPR&D charge to R&D; oncology program TTI-622 (CD47); assets and liabilities assumed noted.

- Divestitures:
  - Meridian (2021): sold for ~$51M; ~$167M loss recorded in discontinued operations; entered TSAs (generally 12–18 months) and a manufacturing supply agreement (3 years plus potential 2-year extension); no amounts recorded under these arrangements in 2021.
  - Upjohn separation and combination with Mylan to form Viatris (2020): Reverse Morris Trust; pro rata distribution (~0.124079 Viatris shares per Pfizer share); post-transaction ownership ~57% Pfizer stockholders/43% Mylan shareholders; generally tax-free. Upjohn entities issued ~$11.4B in notes plus other facilities to fund a $12.0B cash distribution to Pfizer; Pfizer used proceeds to retire debt. Interest on Upjohn debt recorded in discontinued operations. Spin-off effects included distribution of ~$1.6B net assets reducing retained earnings, AOCI increase of ~$423M reclassified to retained earnings, and separation-related costs ($434M in 2020; $83M in 2019). Pfizer is no longer obligor/guarantor of Upjohn debt.

nodes.title: Array
nodes.heading: Array
nodes.start_phrase: On July 30, 2019, we acquired Array, a commercial stage biopharmaceutical company focused on the discovery, development and commercialization of targeted small moleculemedicines to treat cancer and other diseases of high unmet need, for $48 per share in cash.
nodes.summary:
- Acquisition accounting for Array BioPharma (2019): final purchase price allocation completed in 2020, recording $6.3B of identifiable intangibles (developed technology rights with finite lives, IPR&D, and licensing agreements—both indefinite- and finite-lived), $6.1B of goodwill, $1.1B of net deferred tax liabilities, and $451M of assumed debt (repaid in 2019). 2020 measurement period adjustments reduced identifiable intangibles by about $900M with corresponding changes to goodwill and deferred taxes, with no material impact on 2020 income.
- Array portfolio context: includes Braftovi and Mektovi, a broad oncology pipeline, and out-licensed medicines with potential milestone and royalty streams.
- Therachon (2019): treated as an asset acquisition focused on an achondroplasia asset; $340M upfront plus up to $470M milestones; total consideration fair value of $322M (including a prior $5M investment); recorded a $337M charge to R&D.
- Divestiture of Meridian (Dec 31, 2021): sold for approximately $51M cash; recognized a net loss of about $167M within discontinued operations. Post-sale arrangements include short-term transition services (12–18 months) and a manufacturing supply agreement (3 years with a 2-year extension); no 2021 amounts recorded under these agreements.
- Upjohn separation and combination with Mylan to form Viatris (Nov 16, 2020): executed via a Reverse Morris Trust. Pfizer distributed Viatris shares to its shareholders (about 0.124079 Viatris share per Pfizer share), then Upjohn combined with Mylan; post-transaction ownership ~57% Pfizer shareholders and ~43% Mylan shareholders; generally expected to be tax-free for U.S. purposes. Viatris operates as a standalone public company (VTRS).
- Transaction financing: Upjohn entities issued ~$11.4B of senior notes and arranged additional facilities to fund a $12.0B cash distribution to Pfizer. Pfizer used proceeds to reduce commercial paper and redeem certain notes early; related 2020 interest expense reported in discontinued operations. After the separation, Pfizer is no longer an obligor/guarantor of Upjohn debt.
- Equity and AOCI impacts from the Upjohn spin-off: distribution of $1.6B of net assets reduced retained earnings (including a referenced change to MTM accounting in 2021); $412M of cash was transferred with the remainder non-cash. A net $423M increase to accumulated other comprehensive loss reflected derecognition of FX translation gains and benefit plan credits reclassified to retained earnings.
- Separation-related costs for Upjohn: $434M in 2020 and $83M in 2019, primarily for professional and banking fees, recorded in discontinued operations.

to $470million contingent on the achievement of key milestones in the development and commercialization of the lead asset.

Notes 2020 measurement period adjustments reduced identifiable intangibles by about $900 million with corresponding changes to goodwill and deferred taxes, with no material impact on 2020 earnings.
- Details the July 1, 2019 Therachon transaction, accounted for as an asset acquisition focused on an achondroplasia program: $340 million upfront plus up to $470 million in milestones; total consideration fair value of $322 million (including a prior $5 million investment), and recognition of a $337 million R&D expense.
- Outlines divestiture of Meridian on December 31, 2021 for approximately $51 million in cash, with a loss of about $167 million recorded in discontinued operations. Post-sale arrangements include transitional services agreements (12–18 months) and a manufacturing supply agreement (3 years plus a 2-year extension), with no amounts recorded in 2021.
- Explains the November 16, 2020 separation of the Upjohn Business and combination with Mylan to form Viatris via an all-stock Reverse Morris Trust: Pfizer shareholders received approximately 0.124079 Viatris shares per Pfizer share; Mylan shareholders received one Viatris share per Mylan share. Viatris paid Pfizer $12.0 billion prior to the distribution; post-close ownership was ~57% Pfizer shareholders and ~43% Mylan shareholders. Transaction expected to be tax-free for U.S. purposes.
- Notes Upjohn-related financings in June 2020 totaling about $11.4 billion of senior unsecured notes plus a $600 million delayed draw term loan and a $4.0 billion revolver, used to fund Viatris’s $12.0 billion distribution to Pfizer. Pfizer used proceeds to reduce commercial paper and redeem $1.15 billion (2021 maturity) and $342 million (2023 maturity) of notes early. Related 2020 interest expense recorded in discontinued operations. After the separation, Pfizer is no longer an obligor or guarantor on Upjohn debt.

- Discloses separation-related costs of $434 million in 2020 and $83 million in 2019, primarily professional and advisory fees, recorded in discontinued operations.

  - Reflected a change to mark-to-market accounting (Note 1C).
  - Increased accumulated other comprehensive loss by $423M due to derecognition of $397M FX translation gains and $26M prior service credits, reclassified to retained earnings.

  - Therachon (July 1, 2019): asset acquisition focused on achondroplasia; $340M upfront plus up to $470M milestones; total consideration fair value $322M (including prior $5M investment); $337M R&D expense recognized.

- Divestitures:
  - Meridian (Dec 31, 2021): sold for ~$51M cash; recognized ~$167M after‑tax loss in discontinued operations; entered TSAs (12–18 months) and an MSA (3 years with 2‑year extension); no amounts recorded under these in 2021.
  - Upjohn separation and combination with Mylan to form Viatris (Nov 16, 2020): Reverse Morris Trust with pro rata distribution (0.124079 Viatris share per Pfizer share); Viatris paid Pfizer $12.0B pre‑distribution; post‑close ownership ~57% Pfizer stockholders / ~43% former Mylan shareholders; expected tax‑free. Upjohn entities issued ~$11.4B of notes plus other facilities to fund the $12.0B payment; Pfizer used proceeds to repay commercial paper and redeem certain notes; related 2020 interest expense included in discontinued operations. Pfizer no longer obligor/guarantor of Upjohn debt. Accounting effects: distributed net assets of $1.6B (reduction to retained earnings); AOCI increased $423M (FX translation gains and benefit plan credits reclassified to retained earnings); separation costs of $434M (2020) and $83M (2019) in discontinued operations. Post‑transaction agreements (agency arrangements, MSAs for 4–7 years, TSAs up to 3 years, tax and employee matters); amounts not material. Net amounts due from Viatris: $53M (2021) vs $401M (2020); a $277M payment in 2021 classified in other financing activities.

- Discontinued operations:
  - 2021 primarily reflects Meridian operations (including a $345M pre‑tax EpiPen MDL charge) and the $167M after‑tax loss on sale; also minor impacts from the Mylan‑Japan collaboration and post‑closing adjustments related to former Upjohn and Nutrition businesses.
  - 2020 and 2019 reflect operations of Upjohn, Meridian, and Mylan‑Japan; 2020 includes $116M pre‑tax interest on Upjohn notes and $223M pre‑tax charge for Euro debt remeasurement.
  - Disclosure of assets and liabilities of discontinued operations and assets held for sale at year‑end 2021 and 2020.

- Equity‑method investments:
  - Consumer Healthcare JV with GSK (closed July 31, 2019): Pfizer received a 32% stake and deconsolidated its Consumer Healthcare business; recognized an $8.1B pre‑tax gain ($5.4B net of tax). No operating contribution in 2021 or 2020. Investment valued via discounted cash flow; carried at $16.3B (2021) vs $16.7B (2020), with the decrease driven by $499M in dividends and $384M FX translation losses, partly offset by Pfizer’s share of earnings.
  - Pfizer records its share of JV earnings on a one‑quarter lag in Other (income)/deductions—net: $495M recorded in 2021; $417M in 2020; $47M in 2019.
  - Initial basis difference of ~$4.8B allocated to inventory, definite‑ and indefinite‑lived intangibles, related deferred taxes, and equity‑method goodwill; amortization recognized in Other (income)/deductions—net (inventory portion completed by Q2 2020; definite‑lived intangibles amortized over 8–20 years).
  - Summarized JV financial position provided as of September 30, 2021 and 2020.

nodes.title: Equity-Method Investments
nodes.heading: C. Equity-Method Investments
nodes.start_phrase:
On July 31, 2019, we completed a transaction in which we and GSK combined our respective consumer healthcare businesses into a new JV
 that operates globally under the GSKConsumer Healthcare name.
nodes.summary:
- Describes Pfizer’s formation of a Consumer Healthcare joint venture (JV) with GSK on July 31, 2019, under the GSK Consumer Healthcare name; Pfizer holds 32% and GSK 68%.
- Notes deconsolidation of Pfizer’s Consumer Healthcare business at closing and recognition of a pre-tax gain of $8.1 billion ($5.4 billion net of tax) in Q3 2019, reflecting the difference between the fair value of Pfizer’s 32% stake and the carrying value of the business.
- Explains that 2019 results include seven months of domestic and eight months of international Consumer Healthcare operations; 2020 and 2021 results exclude the business.
- Details equity-method accounting for the JV, with valuation using discounted cash flow techniques and key assumptions on projected cash flows (including competitive/legal/regulatory effects), long-term growth, discount rate, and tax rate.
- Reports carrying value of Pfizer’s JV investment: $16.3 billion at December 31, 2021 and $16.7 billion at December 31, 2020, classified as a private equity investment within Equity-method investments.
- Indicates the JV is a foreign investee with GBP reporting currency; foreign currency translation adjustments affect the investment’s carrying value and other comprehensive income. The 2021 decrease reflects $499 million of dividends and $384 million of pre-tax FX translation losses, partially offset by Pfizer’s share of JV earnings.
- States Pfizer records its share of JV earnings on a one-quarter lag in Other (income)/deductions—net starting August 1, 2019; Pfizer’s recognized share: $495 million in 2021, $417 million in 2020, and $47 million in 2019.
- Outlines initial basis difference at formation: estimated fair value of $15.7 billion vs. Pfizer’s 32% share of the JV’s carrying value at $11.2 billion (later revised to $11.0 billion), resulting in a basis difference increasing from ~$4.5 billion to ~$4.8 billion.
- Explains allocation of basis difference primarily to inventory, definite- and indefinite-lived intangible assets, related deferred tax liabilities, and equity-method goodwill; amortization recognized in Other (income)/deductions—net and not material. Inventory-related amortization completed by Q2 2020; definite-lived intangibles amortized over 8–20 years.
- Notes Consumer Healthcare pre-tax income within Pfizer through July 31, 2019 was $654 million.
- Provides summarized JV balance sheet data (as of September 30, 2021 vs. 2020): total assets $46.3B vs. $45.0B; total liabilities $10.4B vs. $10.6B; equity attributable to shareholders $35.7B vs. $34.2B; noncontrolling interests $0.3B vs. $0.2B.

nodes.title: Formation of Consumer Healthcare JV
nodes.heading: Formation of Consumer Healthcare JV
nodes.start_phrase:
On July 31, 2019, we completed a transaction in which we and GSK combined our respective consumer healthcare businesses into a new JV
 that operates globally under the GSKConsumer Healthcare name.
nodes.summary:
- Equity-method investments—Consumer Healthcare JV with GSK:
  - On July 31, 2019, Pfizer and GSK combined consumer healthcare businesses into a JV (GSK Consumer Healthcare); Pfizer holds 32%, GSK 68%.
  - Pfizer deconsolidated the business and recognized a pre-tax gain of $8.1 billion ($5.4 billion net of tax) in Q3 2019. Pfizer’s 2019 results include seven months of U.S. and eight months of international Consumer Healthcare operations; no contribution in 2020 or 2021.
  - Investment accounted for under the equity method; valued using discounted cash flow techniques (key assumptions: projected cash flows, long-term growth, discount rate, tax rate).
  - Carrying value: $16.3 billion at Dec 31, 2021 (vs. $16.7 billion at Dec 31, 2020), reported as a private equity investment within Equity-method investments. The JV reports in GBP; foreign currency translation adjustments recorded in OCI and the investment balance.
  - 2021 decrease primarily from $499 million in dividends and $384 million pre-tax FX translation adjustments, partially offset by Pfizer’s share of JV earnings.
  - Pfizer records its share of JV earnings on a one-quarter lag in Other (income)/deductions—net: $495 million recorded in 2021; $417 million in 2020; $47 million recorded in Q4 2019 for two months of Q3 2019.
  - Initial fair value at close: $15.7 billion; Pfizer’s 32% share of carrying value of JV net assets initially $11.2 billion (later revised to $11.0 billion), creating a basis difference of ~$4.8 billion allocated primarily to inventory, definite- and indefinite-lived intangibles, related deferred taxes, and equity-method goodwill.
  - Amortization of basis differences recorded in Other (income)/deductions—net; inventory-related amortization completed by Q2 2020; definite-lived intangibles amortized over 8–20 years; impact not material.
  - 2019 Consumer Healthcare (pre-JV) pre-tax income through July 31, 2019: $654 million.
  - Summarized JV financials (most recent available):
    - As of Sept 30, 2021: total assets $46.3B; total liabilities $10.4B; equity attributable to shareholders $35.7B.
    - Twelve months ended Sept 30, 2021: net sales $12.8B; net income $1.6B.

- Investment in ViiV (HIV company formed with GSK in 2009):
  - Pfizer owns ~11.7%. Equity method applied prior to 2016; suspended in 2016 when carrying value was reduced to zero from cumulative losses/dividends.
  - Since 2016, dividends recognized in Other (income)/deductions—net: $166 million (2021), $278 million (2020), $220 million (2019).
  - Summarized ViiV financials:
    - As of Dec 31, 2021: total assets $7.2B; total liabilities $10.0B; shareholders’ deficit $(2.9)B.
    - Year ended Dec 31, 2021: net sales $6.4B; net income $2.0B.

- Licensing arrangements:
  - Valneva (Lyme disease vaccine VLA15):
    - Agreement signed Apr 30, 2020 to co-develop/commercialize; Valneva eligible for up to $308 million (including $130 million upfront expensed in Q2 2020 R&D, $35 million development milestones, $143 million early commercialization milestones).
    - Valneva funds 30% of development costs; Pfizer leads late-stage development and commercialization; Valneva receives tiered royalties.
  - Akcea (Ionis subsidiary) — AKCEA-ANGPTL3-LRx:
    - Worldwide exclusive license signed Oct 4, 2019; $250 million upfront expensed in Q4 2019 R&D.
    - On Jan 31, 2022, Pfizer and Ionis discontinued the Pfizer-led program and Pfizer returned rights to Ionis.

nodes.title: Collaborative Arrangements
nodes.heading: E. Collaborative Arrangements
nodes.start_phrase: We enter into collaborative arrangements with respect to in-line medicines, as well as medicines in development that require completion of research and regulatory approval.
nodes.summary:
- The section describes Pfizer’s collaborative arrangements, which are contracts with third parties to jointly research, develop, and/or commercialize medicines. These arrangements vary by deal but generally involve both parties actively participating and sharing significant risks, costs, and rewards, including co-promotion, co-development, manufacturing, distribution, and profit sharing.

- Beam Therapeutics (Dec 24, 2021): Multi-year research collaboration using in vivo base editing (mRNA/LNP) for three undisclosed rare disease targets (liver, muscle, CNS). Beam leads research through development candidate selection; Pfizer may opt in for exclusive licenses. Beam can opt in after Phase 1/2 for one program to co-develop/co-commercialize with a 65%/35% (Pfizer/Beam) split of profits and costs. Pfizer expensed a $300 million upfront in Q4 2021; up to $1.05 billion in additional milestones (total up to $1.35 billion if all options exercised); Beam eligible for sales royalties.

- Arvinas (July 21, 2021): Global collaboration for ARV-471 (oral PROTAC ER degrader) in breast cancer. Pfizer paid $650 million upfront and made a $350 million equity investment; recognized $706 million in R&D expense in Q3 2021 (upfront plus equity premium). Arvinas eligible for up to $400 million in approval milestones and $1 billion in commercial milestones. Worldwide 50/50 sharing of development costs, commercialization expenses, and profits. Pfizer held a 6.5% equity stake at Dec 31, 2021.

- Myovant (Dec 26, 2020): Joint development and commercialization of Orgovyx (advanced prostate cancer) and Myfembree (women’s health) in the U.S. and Canada. Pfizer declined an option to commercialize relugolix in oncology outside the U.S./Canada (excluding certain Asian countries). Parties share profits and allowable expenses equally; Myovant covers Pfizer’s share of allowable expenses up to $100 million in 2021 and $50 million in 2022. Pfizer records its share of gross profits as Alliance revenue. Myovant leads regulatory, supply, and Myfembree clinical development. Myovant eligible for up to $4.35 billion (including $650 million upfront paid in Dec 2020; $200 million regulatory milestones for Myfembree—$100 million paid July 2021 and recorded as developed technology rights; and up to $3.5 billion tiered sales milestones). In 2020, Pfizer recognized $499 million as developed technology rights and $151 million in R&D expense for the upfront allocation.

- CStone (Sept 29, 2020): Strategic collaboration focused on oncology in China, including a $200 million upfront equity investment, development/commercialization of sugemalimab (PD-L1 antibody) in mainland China, and a framework to bring additional oncology assets to Greater China. Closed Oct 9, 2020. Pfizer held a 9.8% equity stake at Dec 31, 2021.

- BioNTech – shingles vaccine (Dec 30, 2021): New agreement to develop an mRNA-based shingles vaccine using BioNTech’s mRNA and Pfizer’s antigen technology. Pfizer to pay $225 million (including $75 million upfront cash and $150 million equity); BioNTech eligible for up to $200 million in milestones; BioNTech to pay Pfizer $25 million for antigen technology. Net upfront recorded to R&D expense in Q4 2021. Development costs shared; Pfizer has commercialization rights worldwide except Germany, Turkey, and certain developing countries where BioNTech holds rights. Gross profits to be shared.

- BioNTech – COVID-19 vaccine (Apr 9, 2020): Global co-development of BNT162b2. Pfizer made a $72 million upfront payment and a $113 million equity investment; recognized $98 million in R&D expense in Q2 2020 (upfront plus equity premium). BioNTech eligible for up to $563 million in milestones (total consideration $748 million). After approval and commercialization, Pfizer and BioNTech share gross profits and development costs equally.

nodes.title: Collaboration with Beam

- Collaboration with Arvinas (7/21/2021):

  - $706 million recognized in R&D expense in Q3 2021 (upfront plus equity premium).

  - Pfizer held 6.5% equity in Arvinas as of 12/31/2021.

- Collaboration with Myovant (12/26/2020):
  - Joint U.S./Canada development and commercialization of Orgovyx (advanced prostate cancer) and Myfembree (women’s health).
  - Option for oncology ex-U.S./Canada (excluding certain Asian countries) declined by Pfizer.

  - 2020 accounting: $499 million to Identifiable intangible assets—Developed technology rights and $151 million to R&D expense (allocation of upfront to approved vs. unapproved indications).

- Collaboration with CStone (9/29/2020):
  - Strategic oncology partnership in China: $200 million upfront equity investment; development/commercialization of sugemalimab (PD-L1) in mainland China; framework to bring additional oncology assets to Greater China.
  - Closed 10/9/2020; Pfizer held 9.8% equity in CStone as of 12/31/2021.

- Collaborations with BioNTech:
  - Shingles vaccine (12/30/2021):
    - Agreement to develop mRNA-based shingles vaccine using BioNTech mRNA tech and Pfizer antigen tech.
    - Pfizer to pay $225 million total ($75 million upfront, $150 million equity); BioNTech eligible for up to $200 million in milestones; BioNTech to pay Pfizer $25 million for antigen tech.
    - Net upfront recorded to R&D expense in Q4 2021; shared development costs; Pfizer commercialization rights worldwide except Germany, Turkey, and certain developing countries; profit share on commercialization.
  - COVID-19 vaccine BNT162b2 (4/9/2020):

    - $98 million recognized in R&D expense in Q2 2020 (upfront plus equity premium).
    - Milestones up to $563 million (total potential $748 million).

nodes.title: Collaboration with Arvinas

  - Milestones: up to $400 million (approvals) and up to $1 billion (commercial).
  - Equal sharing of worldwide development costs, commercialization expenses, and profits.
  - Pfizer held a 6.5% Arvinas equity stake as of Dec 31, 2021.

- Myovant (Dec 26, 2020):
  - Joint development/commercialization of Orgovyx (advanced prostate cancer) and Myfembree (women’s health) in the U.S. and Canada.
  - Pfizer declined option to commercialize relugolix in oncology outside the U.S./Canada (excluding certain Asian countries).
  - Equal profit and allowable expense sharing; Myovant covers Pfizer’s share of allowable expenses up to $100 million (2021) and $50 million (2022).
  - Pfizer records its share of gross profits as Alliance revenue; Myovant leads regulatory, supply, and Myfembree clinical development.
  - Myovant eligible for up to $4.35 billion: $650 million upfront (paid Dec 2020), $200 million in regulatory milestones for Myfembree (women’s health; $100 million paid July 2021 and recorded as identifiable intangible assets—developed technology rights), and up to $3.5 billion in tiered sales milestones.

Key collaborations and accounting:

- Arvinas (July 21, 2021): Global co-dev/commercialization of ARV-471 (oral PROTAC ER degrader). Pfizer paid $650M upfront plus $350M equity (6.5% stake at 12/31/21); $706M recognized in R&D for upfront and equity premium. Up to $400M approval and $1B commercial milestones; 50/50 share of development, commercialization costs and profits.
- Myovant (Dec 26, 2020): Joint U.S./Canada development and commercialization of Orgovyx (prostate cancer) and Myfembree (women’s health). 50/50 profit/allowable expense share; Myovant temporarily bears Pfizer’s share up to $100M (2021) and $50M (2022). Pfizer records share of gross profits as Alliance revenue. Myovant eligible up to $4.35B (including $650M upfront, $200M regulatory milestones—$100M paid July 2021 recorded as identifiable intangible—and up to $3.5B tiered sales milestones). 2020 accounting: $499M identifiable intangible (developed technology rights) and $151M R&D expense allocation.
- CStone (Sept 29, 2020): Strategic oncology collaboration in China including $200M equity; development/commercialization of sugemalimab in mainland China and broader Greater China framework. 9.8% equity stake at 12/31/21.
- BioNTech—Shingles (Dec 30, 2021): mRNA shingles vaccine collaboration. Pfizer to pay $225M (including $75M upfront, $150M equity); BioNTech eligible up to $200M in milestones; BioNTech pays Pfizer $25M for antigen technology. Net upfront expensed to R&D in Q4 2021. Shared development costs; Pfizer commercialization rights worldwide except Germany, Turkey, and certain developing countries; profit share.
- BioNTech—COVID-19 (Apr 9, 2020; amended Jan 29, 2021): Co-development of BNT162b2. Initial $72M upfront and $113M equity (additional $50M equity July 2020); $98M R&D expense for upfront/premium. Milestones up to $563M (total consideration $748M). Post-approval, 50/50 gross profit and R&D cost sharing; Pfizer initially bore all pre-commercialization R&D with BioNTech repaying 50% via lump sum in Q1 2021. Commercialization: Pfizer rights ex-Germany/Turkey (BioNTech) and ex-China/HK/Macau/Taiwan (Fosun). Summarized financials for collaborations (millions):
